A Primer for Players
ALTERRA
THE LAST DAYS OF THE AGE OF GIANTS

At Haltendorf the bells ring for the dead every evening, and every evening someone new is listening. The gatekeeper offers you bread and salt before he asks your name. He states the terms aloud: three nights beneath the city's protection, and no longer unless the Chapter renews it. A herald repeats them so that no one can later remember them differently. Beyond the walls, past a field of headstones packed so close a child could walk on them, the cathedral rises. Somewhere beneath it a knight older than the war is dreaming. Somewhere beyond the hills, something that should be extinct has learned to hunt.

Alterra is a country built around promises. Its people inherit a courtly civilization of heralds, saints, knightly orders, formal hospitality, and carefully witnessed oaths. They also inherit the knowledge that these same virtues once divided the country and armed a war between its patron gods. Courtesy survives here not as decoration, but as a discipline intended to keep disagreement from becoming another sacred catastrophe.

The gods of Alterra are dead.
Their laws are not.
Their blood still walks the earth.

Part I
The Setting at a Glance
A wounded chivalric culture
Alterrans still believe in honor, mercy, courage, hospitality, loyalty, and truth. They no longer believe those virtues always agree.
Dead patrons, living blood
The twin gods Aurel and Valen killed one another in the skies above the valley. Their blood fell as burning rain and changed the land, the beasts, and some of the people.
The last living wonders
Divine blood once made animals into immense Godblooded Beasts. Most lineages are believed extinct. The survivors are known by name and treated as relics, neighbors, weapons, or disasters.
Orders without an age
Five great knightly orders outlived the gods, the kings, and the creatures that gave them purpose. They now disagree over which duties remain.
A crown without a kingdom
Prince Lucan Ardel intends to reunify Alterra, reopen its roads, and replace centuries of divided stewardship with a single mortal government.
A closed valley opening
Alterra lies in a mountain-ringed basin. For generations almost no one came in. The reopened Gold Road is about to change that.
A future arriving early
Creatures believed extinct have begun to appear again, younger and more violent than the Beasts recorded in old songs.
Part II
Your Road In

The campaign begins with the first serious merchant caravan to attempt the newly reopened Gold Road. It climbs out of the world beyond the mountains, threads the narrow approach through the Westreach, and comes down to Haltendorf, the fortified gateway to the valley. Nothing passes into Alterra without passing Haltendorf first.

The First Caravan
Size
Forty wagons and a hundred and sixty souls, larger than any trade venture in living memory
Cargo
Dyes, glass, iron, medicines, seed grain, and sealed letters
Authority
The Gold Road Compact, Prince Lucan's agreement fixing the tolls, the escorts, and a single legal process for disputes along the route
Caravan master
Anselm Querre, a foreign factor
Compact Warden
Dame Elsabet Rook, in Lucan's service, who holds the papers that say the caravan may enter at all
First stop
Haltendorf, the City of Saints

Characters may be guards, scouts, merchants, pilgrims, scholars, rare foreign representatives, or Alterrans returning home. They enter a country arguing about its future and soon encounter evidence that its understanding of the present is dangerously incomplete.

What to Expect
Road travel Courtly disputes Monster hunts Religious disagreement Lost orderhouses Disputed history Duties that conflict

Expect choices in which more than one honorable duty may be true. Alterra rewards characters who accept responsibility, even when they disagree about what justice requires.

Part III
The Godswar and the Age of Giants

For most of its remembered history, Alterra stood beneath the protection of twin gods. Other gods were worshipped too, but the twins were the divine authors of Alterra's civic character.

Aurel
The Remembering Voice
Song, memory, lament, beauty, and the preservation of worthy deeds.
Colors: gold and white
Valen
The Unbroken Word
Honor, duty, judgment, courage, and the obligations created by freely given promises.
Colors: grey and iron

Under the twins, a ruler justified authority through stewardship. A knight submitted strength to service. Heralds protected names from slander, and poets preserved the deeds of enemies as well as friends.

The War of Two Virtues

No surviving account explains why the brothers turned upon one another. Three traditions survive:

  1. Aurel revealed a truth that Valen had sworn must remain hidden.
  2. Valen enforced an oath Aurel believed had become unjust.
  3. Mortals divided first and drew their patrons into the quarrel.

Alterrans agree only that the gods demanded allegiance and the country obeyed. Orders split. Families divided. Songs became propaganda, and vows became permission to continue long after mercy should have intervened.

The war ended only when the brothers struck one another down in the skies above the valley. Their blood fell across Alterra in burning rain. Fishermen still give a wide berth to Godfall Isle in the Sea of Sorrows, where something fell hard enough to open the earth.

Neither army surrendered. Neither god named a victor. Local truces became permanent borders, and the survivors went on defending causes whose divine authors no longer existed. Families rarely announce which god their ancestors followed, but the answer survives in heraldic colors, feast days, burial positions, and the verses people conspicuously refuse to sing.

The Age of Giants

The blood did not stay where it fell. It entered rivers, stone, roots, weather, animals, and people. A red-veined cliff may carry whispers across a valley. A spring may heal one traveler and mark another for life. Flowers may open only when an oath is spoken nearby.

The most famous transformations were the Godblooded Beasts. For generations, horned giants pulled fortress wagons, raptor packs carried mounted companies, and great Tyrants served as royal weapons and order symbols. The knightly orders learned to track, tend, ride, contain, and hunt them. Beast riders became the heroes of the age, though they were always rarer than the songs suggest.

Then, slowly, the lineages seemed to fail. No host of raptor cavalry remains. No order can field a line of Tyrant riders. For decades Alterra has been preparing for what it believes will be the quiet end of its living wonders.

Part IV
Manners, Oaths, and Songs

Alterra did not become less courtly after the Godswar. It became more deliberately so. Formal greetings, witnessed apologies, precise accusations, sanctuary, and safe conduct are the social armor of a people who know how quickly righteous disagreement becomes holy violence.

An Alterran may despise a guest and still offer bread, salt, and a protected place by the fire. To refuse those courtesies is to declare that ordinary civilization no longer stands between you.

The Wounded Virtues

Children still learn the traditional virtues, but each lesson now includes its failure.

Virtue
Can become
Honor
Inflexibility
Loyalty
Faction
Courage
Vanity paid for by other people
Mercy
Favoritism
Truth
Words spoken solely to inflame hatred
Piety
An excuse to surrender judgment to a stronger power

The admired Alterran is not someone who never doubts, but someone who can hold several duties at once, see who will bear the cost, and remain accountable afterward.

Oaths and the Three Questions

Serious vows are witnessed, recorded, and limited. Before accepting a grave duty, a knight is asked three questions:

I
Whom does the duty serve?
II
Who may suffer from its fulfillment?
III
What would release you from it?

A person who cannot answer the third question is not considered exceptionally loyal. They are considered dangerous.

Accusations

Four words make four different accusations, each graver than the last:

1
Mistaken
2
Dishonorable
3
Oath-breaking
4
Faithless

Challenges and feuds have recognized forms, because procedure gives anger time to cool and witnesses time to intervene. Unannounced violence carries more shame than violence openly declared and properly answered.

Songs and Dangerous Memory

A song may be entertainment, prayer, genealogy, legal evidence, or political threat. Wartime ballads survive in contradictory versions naming different heroes and crimes. Certain verses are forbidden at particular courts, because everyone understands what performing them would accuse the host of believing.

Saints and Other Gods

With the patrons dead and other gods held at careful distance, devotion turned toward saints, ancestors, and exemplary mortals. A saint need not work miracles. The title may belong to anyone remembered for choosing rightly when law, loyalty, and survival pointed in different directions. Roadside shrines name ferrymen, healers, deserters, queens, stablehands, and condemned knights.

The wider pantheon still heals, buries, and blesses, and its miracles are real. Alterrans regard those gods somewhat as they regard foreign sovereigns: legitimate and powerful, yet not wholly theirs. A miracle proves that a god has power. It does not prove that the god has wisdom.

Customs an Outsider Notices
Bread and salt establish temporary protection. The host states its duration and limits and cannot withdraw it without formal cause.
A third voice witnesses important promises, repeating the terms aloud.
Songs are introduced by origin. Naming who taught you a song and where its version comes from is basic courtesy.
Authority must be useful. A noble who cannot defend roads, feed dependents, or submit to judgment may keep a title and lose all respect.
Heraldic colors are read closely. Gold-and-white and grey-and-iron are rarely worn together, and almost never by accident.
Part V
The Great Orders

The orders are not merely bands of armored warriors. Since the Godswar they have guarded roads, treated the wounded, kept records, buried the dead, arbitrated disputes, tended Beasts, and trained specialists. None claims to govern Alterra, yet together they do much of the work of a state. Each now faces a prince who may absorb its authority just as the returning Beasts revive its oldest purpose.

The Unbroken Lance
Seat: Targos
Stand between violence and those unable to withstand it.
Once famous for Tyrant riders. Openly divided over serving Lucan and over whether the new Beasts must be destroyed.
The Far Lantern
Seat: Goldcoast Watch
Leave no traveler to die upon the road.
Keeps waystations and road-lamps across the basin. Supports common road law but fears becoming a royal patrol.
The Unbroken Chorus
Seat: Koss
Bear true witness even to an enemy's deeds.
Holds the contested records of succession and Beast lineages. Its Reliquary Knight no longer answers.
The Open Hand
Seat: the shrine on the Titan's back
Offer mercy before judgment.
Tends the surviving Beasts. Demands that newborn creatures be studied before they are hunted.
The Hollow Bell
Seat: Haltendorf
Give every dead soul a name and a place.
Guards graves, crypts, and awakening rites. Opposes using the dead to manufacture political legitimacy.
The Reliquary Knights

Before the Godblooded Beasts existed, each great order preserved one dying champion inside an immense sacred reliquary. The armor is a tomb and a life-support, not a weapon. A Reliquary Knight cannot fight. Most sleep in a deep coma and can be woken only briefly, at real risk, to answer questions or give judgment.

They remember old Alterra and, in some cases, the Godswar itself. They know the Age of Giants only through what later generations chose to tell them. Each order controls access to its own knight, and every awakening is part sacrament, part interview, and part political struggle. Prince Lucan needs them, because the lawful reach of the ancient crown and the wording of the coronation oath may survive only in their memories.

Part VI
The Land and the Gold Road
Alterra: the enclosed basin, its two seas, and the Gold Road entering at Haltendorf.

Alterra is an enclosed basin ringed by the Westreach and the World's Wall Mountains. The Sea of Sorrows, the Sea of Songs, Wyrmrest Lake, Still Lake, and their rivers are all inland waters. Barges carry most heavy cargo between regions, but no foreign ship has ever reached an Alterran shore. For generations, nearly everyone met on these waters has been Alterran.

The Three Cities
Haltendorf THE CITY OF SAINTS
Haltendorf stands where the Gold Road comes down out of the mountains. Every lawful overland traveler passes beneath its walls, so the city is gateway, customs house, quarantine station, fortress, and first impression at once. Its docks on the Sea of Sorrows let admitted goods move through the valley by water. Its cathedral rises from an enormous field of tightly packed headstones, and beneath it lie the Reliquary Knights. Every great order keeps a house or delegation nearby. The Hollow Bell rings the evening bells.
Targos THE HIGH SEAT
Targos holds a defensible rise above the Northrime crossings at the head of the Worldspine, between the two seas. Its concentric walls and broad avenues were built to move mounted companies quickly in the Age of Giants. The royal palace stood mostly empty for generations as neutral ground for councils that rarely agreed. Lucan has made it his headquarters and filled its halls with surveyors, quartermasters, judges, and young officers. To supporters the city feels awake for the first time in living memory. To critics it feels occupied by a government that does not legally exist.
Koss THE CITY OF SONGS
Koss stands on the eastern shore of the Sea of Songs at the head of the Lashar Peninsula. It is Alterra's center of performance, instrument making, legal recitation, and historical argument. A Koss family may own little land and still wield great influence if its singers, advocates, or chroniclers decide how the country remembers a disputed event. Koss does not reject unity, but it insists that no king should decide which verses the country is permitted to remember.
The Road Itself

From Haltendorf the Gold Road runs east along the Gold Coast to Goldcoast Watch, the Far Lantern's great tower, then bends north toward Londorf and the forested slopes below the Shard, a mountain whose upper face gleams like gold-green glass. From there, roads and waterways carry goods on to Targos, to Koss, and to the smaller settlements of the basin: lake ports like Wavecrest and Farcoast Watch, the marsh town of Muldorf, island-walled Riveholme on Still Lake, and Vyrmanthir and Banshear on the Lashar shore.

Few travelers go willingly into the Witchweald, the pale, mist-bound forest in the southeast, or past Lonebrook at its edge.

The Titan's Circuit

The greatest known Beast is an ancient, long-necked creature called the Titan. He walks a slow circuit from Haltendorf to Targos, from Targos to Koss, and back to Haltendorf, passing around the Shard as he goes. No rider directs him. A mobile shrine of the Open Hand rests on his back, and its keepers tend his aging joints and lower stairs when he chooses to rest. Each circuit takes longer than the last. The most recent took almost nine years, and he is expected at Haltendorf this season.

Haltendorf
Rings funeral bells when he arrives.
Targos
Turns his arrival into civic ceremony.
Koss
Closes its roads and lays in enormous stores of fodder.

Lucan's heralds call the circuit proof that Alterra has always been one country. His opponents note that the Titan has never bowed to a king.

Part VII
The Crownless Prince

Alterra has had lords, councils, city charters, and temporary war leaders since the Godswar, but no ruler recognized throughout the country. The orders and the cities govern through overlapping custom. That arrangement prevents easy tyranny and makes almost every shared undertaking slow, expensive, and vulnerable to rivalry.

Lucan Ardel is the twenty-seven-year-old heir of the last broadly recognized royal line. His supporters call him the Crownless Prince; his enemies use the same title as a joke. He is educated, personally brave, and unusually attentive to administration. He does not promise to restore the Age of Giants. He argues that Alterra must finally outlive it.

The Gold Road Compact is his first great test. His agents negotiated the tolls, hired the escorts, repaired the bridges, and promised a single legal process for disputes along the route. If the caravan succeeds, it shows that a central authority can manage contact with the outside world before Lucan ever wears a crown. It also gives him revenue independent of the old houses, and a merchant class whose fortunes depend on his reforms.

Why People Follow Him
Merchants want one system: common weights, coinage, tolls, and road law.
Villages want reliable protection, not whichever lord or order can spare riders that season.
Young nobles want a future outside inherited feuds and exhausted estates.
Ordinary people want ordinary government: bridges, courts, grain reserves, and paid soldiers.
Why People Fear Him
Divided authority is partly intentional. It keeps any single conviction from mobilizing the whole country as the gods once did.
A good king may still create powers inherited by a cruel heir.
The orders ask whether they could refuse an unjust royal command; the free cities ask what becomes of their charters.
Old families see confiscation behind reform. Priests see a mortal claiming the unity once reserved for the twins.

Lucan understands these objections and proceeds anyway. That may be his greatest qualification for rule, or the first sign of the danger his enemies describe.

Part VIII
Godblooded Beasts

A Godblooded Beast is an animal the divine blood made immense, strange, and sometimes intelligent. Many resemble creatures known elsewhere only from fossils and legend. Size alone does not make a Beast. Godblood alters behavior, senses, and the land around the creature. A Beast may carry weather in its wake, remember spoken vows, reshape a migration route, or produce young unlike either parent. The same creature could be guardian to one valley and famine to the next.

The Known Survivors

Every educated Alterran can name the great survivors, the way one names the old queens.

The Titan
The ancient keeper of the circuit, tended by the Open Hand.
Grief
The last Tyrant of the Unbroken Lance, blind and riderless, kept in the chapterhouse yards at Targos.
The Pelarch
A storm-winged giant of the air that roosts above Pelarch's Hollow. Fishermen on the Sea of Sorrows read the weather by its flight.
The Sleeper of Wyrmrest
A long-necked swimmer that gave the lake its name. It has not surfaced in sixty years. Some say it is dead. No one says so near Wavecrest.
Brannoc
An aged horned giant that once hauled the fortress wagons of Riveholme, now grazing the shores of Still Lake.

Other, lesser survivors are known locally, and the Witchweald is said to hold things no order has catalogued.

The Births
News that has not yet become official

Travelers report tracks belonging to extinct species, nests where no adults are known to live, and young Beasts showing powers absent from any record. The new creatures are aggressive, territorial, and hard to calm. Most authorities call these stories misidentification, poaching fraud, or panic. Those who have seen the evidence are less certain.

In taverns, several explanations circulate:

  • The young may be hatching without elders to teach them restraint.
  • Settlement may have reached forgotten nesting grounds.
  • Someone may be waking dormant blood on purpose.
  • And some say, quietly, that Aurel and Valen are still at war inside their blood.
Part IX
Beyond the Wall

Alterra can sit inside a much larger world without being culturally absorbed by it. In a Faerûn campaign, the lands beyond the Westreach and the World's Wall are simply the familiar Realms: their gods answer prayer, their peoples and classes exist normally, and their histories continue without Alterra at the center of them.

To most outsiders, Alterra is an old, difficult-to-reach country of contradictory stories: dead local gods, impossible animals, severe mountain passes, and a road that has only now become worth attempting. Foreign characters do not need Alterran ancestry or special lore. The caravan is their reason to arrive, and ignorance of local custom is expected rather than penalized.

For Alterrans, the imbalance runs the other way. A Waterdhavian, Chondathan, dwarf, tiefling, foreign cleric, or other traveler may be familiar to the wider world and still be remarkable here. The reopening of the Gold Road is not only Alterra returning to the world; it is the world arriving in Alterra.

Part X
Making Your Character

Any standard class belongs here. A character need not be courtly, Alterran, or conventionally heroic. Cynics belong here if they care enough to recognize hypocrisy. Criminals belong here if obligations can still reach them. The campaign assumes only that the party will accept shared responsibility when other people are in danger.

Class
Its place in Alterra
Fighters and paladins
Meet competing traditions of knighthood.
Bards
Inherit the political danger of memory.
Clerics
Serve active gods before a people suspicious of divine certainty.
Rangers and druids
Read Godblooded landscapes.
Wizards and sorcerers
Study reliquaries and altered life.
Rogues
Serve as scouts, heralds, smugglers, investigators, relic thieves, or quiet agents of institutions whose public honor leaves certain work unnamed.

Foreign characters are exceptional members of an exceptional expedition; the gatekeepers of Haltendorf will notice them.

Reasons to Join the Caravan
Duty
You swore to protect a traveler, deliver a sealed letter, investigate conditions on the road, or recover something carried along it.
Opportunity
A reopened market promises wealth, patronage, lost craft, royal employment, or a place in a great order.
Pilgrimage
You seek Haltendorf's cathedral, the Titan's shrine, a Reliquary Knight, or the grave of someone whose name still matters.
Exile or Return
You or your family left Alterra, and the Gold Road is a way back into unfinished history.
Conviction
You mean to support Lucan, oppose him, reform an order, defend a free city, or prove Alterra needs a different future.
Wonder
You grew up on stories of the Beasts and refuse to accept that the age is truly over.
Questions for Character Creation

Answer as many or few as you like.

1
What promise have you made that would hurt to keep, and what would release you from it?
2
Which virtue do you admire most, and how have you seen it become harmful?
3
Do you regard the Godblooded Beasts as legends, animals, monsters, holy relics, weapons, or people?
4
What useful change would make you support a king? What abuse would make you resist one?
5
Whose name do you refuse to let the world forget?
The Shape of What Comes

You begin as small participants in a commercial experiment. You may end as witnesses to something every great power in Alterra (and some beyond it) needs to control. The Crown will want your evidence. The orders will claim jurisdiction over it. The merchants will want it quiet, and the villages will want it to stop.

The Age of Giants is not ending quietly. Alterra must decide what deserves to survive it, and so will you.
